papers.title: Neuronal ABHD6 Exacerbates Ischemic Brain Injury Through 2-AG Depletion and DDIT3/BNIP3-Dependent Autophagy Dysregulation
papers.summary: This study investigates how the enzyme ABHD6 in neurons contributes to brain damage after ischemic stroke. It shows that ABHD6 breaks down the molecule 2-AG, and this depletion triggers a stress pathway involving DDIT3 and BNIP3 that disrupts normal autophagy. The result is worsened neuronal damage, suggesting that blocking ABHD6 could be a therapeutic strategy to protect the brain during stroke.
papers.why: This paper is relevant because it details a specific molecular mechanism (DDIT3/BNIP3-dependent autophagy dysregulation) linking lipid signaling to neuronal mitophagy/autophagy control, directly informing the mechanistic framework for studying autophagy dysfunction in neurons.

papers.title: Mitohormesis linking metabolic dysfunction and neurodegeneration: implications for dementia and therapeutic strategies
papers.summary: This paper discusses mitohormesis, a process where mild mitochondrial stress triggers adaptive, protective cellular responses. It explores how disruptions in this balance may link metabolic dysfunction to neurodegenerative diseases, particularly dementia. The authors propose therapeutic strategies that could leverage mitohormetic pathways to protect neurons against degeneration.
papers.why: Understanding mitohormesis provides mechanistic context for how mitochondrial quality control and mitophagy in neurons may go awry during neurodegeneration, directly informing the project's focus on mitophagy dysfunction in brain disease.

papers.title: 1,2-DCE exposure induces autophagosome accumulation and neuronal death via the ROS-JNK/c-Fos/c-Jun/FoxO1/FoxO3a axis.
papers.summary: This study examines how exposure to the industrial chemical 1,2-dichloroethane (1,2-DCE) damages neurons. The researchers found that it causes autophagosomes (structures involved in cellular recycling) to build up abnormally, leading to neuronal death. This toxic effect works through a specific molecular pathway involving reactive oxygen species (ROS), JNK signaling, and the transcription factors c-Fos, c-Jun, FoxO1, and FoxO3a.
papers.why: This paper's focus on how dysregulated autophagy mechanisms (specifically autophagosome accumulation and neuronal death) contribute to neurotoxicity offers mechanistic insight relevant to understanding autophagy/mitophagy dysfunction in neurons, even though it addresses a chemical toxicant rather than the project's primary neuroanatomical focus.

papers.title: Huntingtin Aggregate-Responsive Autophagy Gene Circuit Mitigates Disease Pathology in R6/2 Mice.
papers.summary: This paper describes a synthetic gene circuit designed to detect huntingtin protein aggregates and, in response, trigger autophagy to clear them. The system was tested in R6/2 mice, a well-established model of Huntington's disease, and shown to reduce disease-related pathology. This represents a targeted, aggregate-responsive therapeutic strategy that couples sensing of toxic protein accumulation with activation of the cellular degradation machinery.
papers.why: This work demonstrates an engineered approach to boost autophagy specifically in response to protein aggregates in neurons, directly relevant to studying mitophagy/autophagy dysregulation and potential interventions in neurodegenerative contexts.

papers.title: CBX3 aggravates nucleus pulposus cell apoptosis and extracellular matrix degradation in vitro via repressing SESN2-mediated mitophagy in an H3K9me3-dependent manner.
papers.summary: This study investigates how the protein CBX3 contributes to disc degeneration by promoting nucleus pulposus cell death and breakdown of the extracellular matrix. The mechanism involves CBX3 suppressing SESN2, a gene needed for mitophagy (clearance of damaged mitochondria), through a histone modification called H3K9me3. By blocking this protective mitophagy pathway, CBX3 worsens cellular damage, suggesting it could be a therapeutic target for disc degeneration.
papers.why: While focused on spinal disc cells rather than brain neurons, this paper offers a transferable mechanistic model of H3K9me3-mediated epigenetic repression of SESN2-dependent mitophagy that could inform how analogous pathways regulate mitochondrial quality control in neurons.
